title: Event Loop & Runtime
intro: Almost every senior Node.js interview starts here, because the event loop explains performance, latency spikes and most "why did this run first?" bugs. Interviewers want more than "Node is single-threaded": they want you to name the phases, explain nextTick versus promises versus setImmediate, predict output of tricky snippets, and know how libuv's thread pool and the OS share the work. A senior answer always connects the mechanics to production: what blocks the loop, how you measure it, and how you fix it.

questions.title: Is Node.js single-threaded?
questions.question: People say Node.js is single-threaded. Is that true? How can one thread serve thousands of connections?
questions.short: Your JavaScript runs on one main thread, but Node.js as a process is not single-threaded. Network I/O is handed to the operating system (epoll, kqueue, IOCP), which tells libuv when a socket is ready, so no thread waits on it. Work the OS cannot do asynchronously, like most file system calls, dns.lookup, some crypto and zlib, runs on the libuv thread pool (4 threads by default). The JS thread only runs short callbacks when results are ready, which is why one thread can serve thousands of connections as long as no callback blocks it.
questions.simple: Think of a restaurant with one waiter (the JS thread) and a kitchen full of cooks (the OS and the thread pool). The waiter never stands at the stove; he takes orders, passes them on, and serves dishes when they are ready.

explain.h: Three kinds of "threads" in a Node process

list: The main thread: runs V8, your JavaScript, and the event loop. Only one piece of JS runs at a time here.
The libuv thread pool: a small pool of worker threads (default 4) for blocking work such as `fs.*`, `dns.lookup`, async `crypto.pbkdf2`/`scrypt`/`randomBytes`, and async `zlib`.
The kernel: network sockets, pipes and timers are watched by the OS with epoll (Linux), kqueue (macOS/BSD) or IOCP (Windows). No Node thread is used while waiting for them.

explain.p: There are also a few helper threads you never touch: V8 uses background threads for garbage collection and for optimizing compilers, and the inspector has its own thread. So `top -H` on a Node process shows many threads even for "hello world".

explain.h: Why one JS thread scales for I/O

explain.p: A typical web request spends most of its time waiting: for the database, for another HTTP service, for the disk. Node does not park a thread for each wait. It registers interest with the OS or the pool and moves on. When the result arrives, a small callback runs. 10,000 idle connections cost memory for their sockets and objects, not 10,000 threads.
If you need real parallel JavaScript (CPU-heavy work), you use `worker_threads` (each worker has its own V8 isolate and event loop) or more processes (`cluster`, or several containers).

explain.note: Senior answer in one line: "JavaScript execution is single-threaded; Node.js is not. I/O is concurrent through the OS and the libuv thread pool."

anim.title: The JS thread hands off a file read and keeps going

steps.note: Node loads the module and starts running it on the main thread.
Plain synchronous code runs right away.
fs.readFile does not read the file here. Node asks libuv, and a thread pool worker does the blocking read.
The JS thread did not wait. It keeps running the rest of the script while the worker reads.
The script is done. The stack is empty and the event loop waits in the poll phase, using no CPU.
The worker finishes and tells the loop. The callback is now ready to run.
The event loop calls the callback on the main thread.
Nothing is pending any more, so the loop has no reason to stay alive and the process exits.

followups.q: So is it safe to do CPU-heavy work in a request handler?
followups.a: No. CPU work runs on the main thread and blocks every other request. Move it to worker_threads, a separate service, or break it into chunks.

followups.q: Does an HTTP request use the thread pool?
followups.a: No. Socket reads and writes use the OS event notification (epoll/kqueue/IOCP). Only the DNS lookup for an outgoing request by hostname uses the pool, via dns.lookup.

followups.q: How many threads does a fresh Node process have?
followups.a: Usually around 7 or more: the main thread, V8 platform worker threads for GC and compilation, and others. The 4 libuv pool threads are created lazily the first time the pool is used.

mistakes: Saying "Node is single-threaded, so it cannot do two things at once." I/O happens in parallel; only JS execution is single-threaded.
Thinking every async operation uses the thread pool. Network I/O does not.
Believing async/await makes CPU-heavy code non-blocking. It does not move work off the main thread.

questions.title: Node architecture: V8 vs libuv
questions.question: Walk me through the architecture of Node.js. What does V8 do, and what does libuv do?
questions.short: Node.js is V8 plus libuv glued together by C++ bindings and a JavaScript standard library. V8 parses, compiles and runs JavaScript and manages the heap and garbage collection; it knows nothing about files, sockets or timers. libuv provides the event loop, non-blocking network I/O on top of epoll/kqueue/IOCP, timers, and the thread pool for blocking work. Node's bindings expose libuv and other C/C++ libraries (OpenSSL, zlib, llhttp, c-ares) to JS through modules like fs, net and crypto.
questions.simple: V8 is the engine that understands JavaScript. libuv is the dispatcher that talks to the operating system and tells the engine when something is ready. Node is the car built around both.

head: Layer
What it does
Examples
rows: Bridge between JS and native code
Runs JS: parser, Ignition interpreter, Sparkplug/Maglev/TurboFan JITs, GC
Event loop, async I/O, timers, thread pool, signals, child processes
OpenSSL, zlib, llhttp (HTTP parser), c-ares (DNS), ICU, simdutf

list: V8 owns the call stack, the heap, garbage collection and the Promise microtask queue.
libuv owns the event loop phases, timers, sockets, file requests and the thread pool.
Node itself owns `process.nextTick`, the module loaders, and the logic that drains nextTick and microtasks after each callback.

explain.p: `setTimeout`, `fs` and `http` are not part of JavaScript. They are host APIs. Browsers provide their own versions; Node provides them through libuv and its bindings.

When you call `crypto.pbkdf2(..., cb)`, the JS wrapper validates arguments and calls into C++. The binding creates a job and hands it to libuv's thread pool. When a worker finishes, libuv wakes the event loop, the binding converts the result into a JS Buffer, and V8 runs your callback. Network calls follow the same path, but libuv registers the socket with the kernel instead of using a worker.

explain.note: A good extra point: since a V8 isolate can only run on one thread at a time, `worker_threads` creates a new isolate and a new libuv loop for each worker. That is why workers do not share normal JS objects; they pass messages or share memory via SharedArrayBuffer.

anim.title: One request through the layers

steps.note: listen() goes through the C++ TCP binding. libuv creates a socket and registers it with the kernel (epoll on Linux).
The script ends. libuv sits in the poll phase, blocked in epoll_wait. The process uses no CPU while idle.
A client connects and sends a request. The kernel marks the socket readable and wakes libuv. No thread pool is involved for network I/O.
libuv calls into Node C++, llhttp parses the bytes, and V8 runs your request handler.
pbkdf2 is CPU-heavy, so the binding creates a job and libuv runs it on a thread pool worker.
The handler returns right away. The JS thread is free to accept other requests while the worker hashes.
The worker finishes and signals the loop. The result is waiting to be delivered to JS.
The binding wraps the bytes in a Buffer and V8 runs your callback. res.end() hands the response to the kernel with a non-blocking write.

followups.q: Is the Promise microtask queue part of libuv?
followups.a: No. Microtasks live in V8. Node tells V8 when to run them (after each callback, together with the nextTick queue).

followups.q: What does c-ares do?
followups.a: It implements the dns.resolve*() family with real async network DNS queries, so they do not use the thread pool. dns.lookup() instead calls the OS getaddrinfo() on the thread pool.

followups.q: Where does the event loop live in a worker_thread?
followups.a: Each worker gets its own V8 isolate and its own libuv loop. The libuv thread pool, however, is shared by the whole process.

mistakes: Saying V8 provides setTimeout or fs. They are Node (host) APIs built on libuv.
Calling libuv "the thread pool". The thread pool is only one part of libuv; the event loop and network I/O are the main part.
Forgetting the C++ binding layer, which is where JS values are converted to and from native data.

questions.title: What is the event loop?
questions.question: What is the event loop, in your own words? What does this print: log A, setTimeout B, Promise.then C, log D?
questions.short: The event loop is the loop in libuv that keeps a Node process running: it waits for events (expired timers, finished I/O, setImmediate callbacks) and runs their callbacks on the single JS thread, one at a time, each to completion. Between callbacks Node drains the nextTick queue and the Promise microtask queue. So the snippet prints A, D (synchronous), then C (microtask, right after the current script finishes), then B (a timer, which needs the loop to reach the timers phase).
questions.simple: It is like a cashier with one till. She serves one customer completely, checks a short "urgent" list (microtasks), then calls the next customer from the main line (timers, I/O, immediates).

list: Only one callback runs at a time, and it runs to completion. Nothing interrupts JavaScript in the middle.
Synchronous code (the whole main script, or the whole body of a callback) always finishes first.
When the call stack becomes empty, Node drains `process.nextTick` callbacks, then Promise microtasks, repeating until both are empty.
Only then does the loop move on to the next macrotask: a timer, an I/O callback, a `setImmediate`, a close callback.

explain.p: Because a callback cannot be interrupted, you do not need locks for plain JS objects. A counter `x++` inside a handler is safe. The flip side: a long callback delays everything else, including timers and incoming requests.

The "loop" is literal: libuv's `uv_run()` keeps looping through its phases while there are active, referenced handles (servers, sockets, timers) or pending requests (file reads, DNS lookups). When nothing is left, the loop exits and so does the process.

explain.note: Avoid saying "the event loop runs your code". Your code runs on the call stack inside V8. The event loop decides which callback goes onto the stack next.

anim.title: A, B, C, D: what prints?

steps.note: Synchronous log. It prints right away.
setTimeout only registers a timer (0 becomes 1 ms). The callback waits in the timers list.
The promise is already resolved, so its .then callback goes straight into the microtask queue.
Still synchronous code, so D prints before anything queued.
The main script is finished and the stack is empty. Before the loop moves on, Node drains the microtask queue.
The microtask runs and prints C.
Microtasks are empty. The event loop starts and reaches the timers phase once the 1 ms has passed.
The timer callback runs and prints B.
Nothing is left to wait for, so the loop exits and the process ends.

followups.q: Can a timer interrupt a running loop like while(true)?
followups.a: No. Timers only run when the current callback returns and the loop reaches the timers phase. An infinite loop means the timer never fires.

followups.q: Is the Node event loop the same as the browser one?
followups.a: The idea is the same (one thread, macrotasks, microtasks), but the implementation differs. Node uses libuv phases and adds process.nextTick and setImmediate; browsers have rendering steps and requestAnimationFrame.

mistakes: Thinking setTimeout(fn, 0) runs "immediately". It runs after the current code and all microtasks, in a later timers phase.
Saying the event loop is a separate thread that runs callbacks in parallel with your code.
Forgetting that a resolved promise's .then still runs asynchronously.

questions.title: The event loop phases
questions.question: Name the phases of the Node.js event loop and tell me what runs in each one.
questions.short: Each turn of the loop goes through six phases in order: timers runs expired setTimeout and setInterval callbacks; pending callbacks runs some I/O callbacks deferred from the previous turn, like certain TCP errors; idle/prepare is internal; poll gets new I/O events and runs their callbacks, and is where the loop blocks waiting when nothing else is due; check runs setImmediate callbacks; close callbacks runs handlers like a socket's 'close'. After every single callback, Node drains the nextTick queue and then the microtask queue.
questions.simple: Picture a postman doing the same round every time: first the alarm clocks (timers), then leftover mail, then new mail (poll), then the "right after this" notes (setImmediate), then goodbyes (close).

head: Phase
What runs here
Example
rows: Callbacks of setTimeout/setInterval whose time has passed
Some system I/O callbacks deferred from the previous turn
New I/O events: socket data, finished fs/dns/crypto jobs. May block waiting
Close handlers of handles closed abruptly

explain.p: Poll is the only phase where the loop can sleep. It computes a timeout: if setImmediate callbacks are queued, it does not wait at all; otherwise it waits until the nearest timer is due, or forever if there are no timers but there are active handles (like a listening server). This is why an idle server uses almost no CPU.

Since Node 11, the nextTick queue and the microtask queue are drained after every individual callback, not once per phase. So two setTimeout callbacks due at the same time each get their promise callbacks run before the next one starts. This matches browser behavior.

explain.caption: Pseudo-code, not real Node source

explain.note: process.nextTick and Promise callbacks are not a phase. They run "in between", whenever the JS stack empties.

explain.p: Interview tip: say why the order matters. setImmediate runs right after poll, so from inside an I/O callback it always runs before a new setTimeout(0). Timers are checked at the start of a turn, so their delay is a minimum, not an exact time.

anim.title: One turn of the event loop

steps.note: Imagine this state at the start of a turn: one timer is due, one deferred error, two I/O results ready, one setImmediate, one closed socket.
Timers phase: run every timer whose time has passed. After each callback, nextTick and microtasks are drained.
Pending callbacks: a few system-level I/O callbacks that libuv deferred from the previous turn.
Idle and prepare are internal to libuv and Node. No user callbacks run here.
Poll phase: libuv asks the OS which I/O is ready and runs those callbacks, one by one.
Poll would normally sleep waiting for more I/O, but a setImmediate is queued, so it does not block.
Check phase: setImmediate callbacks run, right after poll.
Close callbacks: handlers like a destroyed socket's 'close' event.
The turn is over. If there are still active referenced handles or requests, a new turn starts; otherwise the loop ends and the process can exit.

followups.q: Where do process.nextTick and promises fit in the phases?
followups.a: Nowhere as a phase. They are drained after each callback in any phase, and after the main script finishes. nextTick first, then microtasks.

followups.q: Why might a setTimeout(fn, 10) fire after 15 ms?
followups.a: The delay is a minimum. The timer only runs when the loop reaches the timers phase, so a busy callback or long poll work delays it.

followups.q: What happens in poll when there is nothing to do?
followups.a: If there are no immediates, libuv blocks in epoll_wait (or the platform equivalent) until I/O arrives or the next timer is due.

mistakes: Listing microtasks or nextTick as a phase.
Saying the microtask queue drains only once per phase. Since Node 11 it drains after every callback.
Forgetting that poll is where the loop sleeps, which is why idle Node servers use no CPU.

questions.title: nextTick vs Promise microtasks
questions.question: What is the difference between macrotasks and microtasks? How does process.nextTick relate to Promise callbacks?
questions.short: Macrotasks are the callbacks the event loop schedules phase by phase: timers, I/O, setImmediate, close handlers. Microtasks are Promise reactions and queueMicrotask callbacks, kept by V8. Node adds a separate nextTick queue. Whenever the JS stack empties, Node first drains the entire nextTick queue, then the entire microtask queue, and repeats until both are empty, before the loop runs the next macrotask. So in a CommonJS script: sync code, then nextTick, then promises, then timers.
questions.simple: Macrotasks are customers in the main line. nextTick is the VIP list and promises are the "quick question" list; both are fully served before the next customer from the main line.

explain.h: The three queues you deal with

head: Queue
Filled by
Owner
When it runs
rows: As soon as the stack empties, first
One callback at a time, by phase

explain.p: Node runs all nextTicks, then all microtasks. If a microtask schedules a nextTick, Node goes back and drains nextTicks again, and so on. Only when both queues are empty does control go back to libuv.

In an ES module (`.mjs` or `"type": "module"`), top-level code itself runs as part of module evaluation, which is driven by promises. When the top-level code finishes, Node is already inside microtask processing, so the promise callback can print before the nextTick. Do not rely on nextTick-vs-promise order across module types.

list: Prefer `queueMicrotask()` or promises for "run after the current code". They are standard and portable.

Use `process.nextTick()` mainly in library code to emit an event or call a callback asynchronously but before any I/O, for example so a user can attach an `error` listener right after creating an object.
Use `setImmediate()` when you want to yield to I/O.

explain.note: The names are confusing: process.nextTick runs sooner than setImmediate. "nextTick" really means "before the loop continues", and "immediate" means "on the next check phase".

anim.title: sync, nextTick, promise, timeout

steps.note: A timer is registered. Its callback is a macrotask and must wait for the timers phase.
The promise is resolved, so its callback goes into V8's microtask queue.
process.nextTick puts the callback in Node's own nextTick queue.
Synchronous code always wins: sync prints first.
The main script is done. Node now drains the nextTick queue first.
The nextTick callback runs.
nextTick queue is empty, so V8 runs the microtask queue.
Both small queues are empty. Now the event loop starts and goes to the timers phase.
The timer callback finally runs.

followups.q: What is queueMicrotask?
followups.a: A standard global that puts a callback straight into the V8 microtask queue, the same queue promises use, without creating a promise.

followups.q: Does the order change in an ES module?
followups.a: It can. In ESM the top-level code runs inside promise-based module evaluation, so pending promise callbacks may run before nextTick callbacks. In CommonJS, nextTick runs first.

followups.q: Why does Node keep process.nextTick if promises exist?
followups.a: Historical and practical reasons: core streams and EventEmitter-based APIs use it to defer callbacks before any I/O, and it is slightly cheaper. The Node docs recommend queueMicrotask for most new code.

mistakes: Saying setImmediate runs before process.nextTick because of the name.
Thinking only one microtask runs between macrotasks. The whole queue is drained, including microtasks added during draining.
Assuming the nextTick-before-promise order holds in ESM too.

questions.title: setTimeout(0) vs setImmediate
questions.question: If I call setTimeout(fn, 0) and setImmediate(fn) together, which runs first?
questions.short: It depends on where you call them. From the main module the order is not deterministic: setTimeout(0) is really 1 ms, and whether that 1 ms has already passed when the loop first checks timers depends on how fast the process started. Inside an I/O callback the order is always setImmediate first, because I/O callbacks run in the poll phase, the next phase is check (setImmediate), and timers only come around on the next turn.
questions.simple: If you are standing in the poll room, the setImmediate room is the next door. The timers room is all the way around the loop.

explain.h: From the main module: a race

explain.p: Node turns a delay of 0 into 1 ms. When the main script finishes, the loop enters the timers phase. If at least 1 ms has passed since the timer was created (based on the loop's cached clock), the timer runs first. If not, the loop moves on through poll to check, runs the immediate, and catches the timer on the next turn. Machine load decides, so the order changes between runs.

explain.h: Inside an I/O callback: always immediate first

explain.p: The readFile callback runs in the poll phase. After poll comes check, so the immediate runs in this same turn. The timer has to wait until the loop wraps around to the timers phase in the next turn.

list: Use `setImmediate` to yield to the event loop "as soon as possible after I/O". It is more predictable and slightly cheaper than `setTimeout(0)`.
Never write code whose correctness depends on the order of setTimeout(0) and setImmediate in the main module.
Timer delays are minimums. A heavy callback can delay any timer.

explain.note: Inside a setImmediate callback, a new setImmediate runs on the next turn, not the current check phase. That is what makes setImmediate safe for chunking work: I/O gets a chance to run between chunks.

anim.title: Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate wins

steps.note: The file read is handed to a thread pool worker.
The main script is done. The loop has nothing else to do, so it waits in the poll phase.
The read finishes. Its callback is ready in the poll phase.
We are now running inside the poll phase.
A 1 ms timer is registered. It can only run in a timers phase.
An immediate is queued for the check phase.
The callback returns. Poll is finished, and the very next phase is check, not timers.
Check phase: the immediate runs. This is guaranteed, no matter how fast the machine is.
Close callbacks (none), then the loop wraps around to the timers phase of the next turn.
The timer runs last.

followups.q: Can you make the main-module case deterministic?
followups.a: Not reliably by timing. If you need a fixed order, chain them: call one from inside the other, or do both from inside an I/O callback.

followups.q: What is the minimum setTimeout delay in Node?
followups.a: 1 ms. Values below 1 (or above 2^31-1) are set to 1 ms. There is no 4 ms clamp like in browsers.

mistakes: Saying setTimeout(0) always runs before setImmediate (or always after).
Explaining the difference with "setImmediate is faster" instead of the phase order.
Thinking a nested setImmediate runs in the same check phase. It runs on the next turn.

questions.title: Puzzle: timers and microtasks
questions.question: What does this code print, and why? (Two timers, a promise that schedules a nextTick, and a top-level nextTick.)
questions.short: It prints 1, 8, 7, 5, 6, 2, 3, 4. First all synchronous logs (1, 8). Then the nextTick queue (7), then the microtask queue (5). The promise callback scheduled a nextTick, so Node drains nextTicks again (6) before going to the loop. In the timers phase, the first timer prints 2 and queues a promise; since Node 11 microtasks drain after each timer callback, so 3 prints before the second timer prints 4.
questions.simple: Finish what you are doing, clear the urgent lists completely (even new urgent items), and only then take the next timer. Repeat after every timer.

explain.h: How to solve any ordering puzzle

list: Step 1: print every synchronous line, top to bottom.
Step 2: drain the nextTick queue completely, then the microtask queue completely. Repeat while either has items, including ones added during draining.
Step 3: move to the event loop phase that has work: timers, then poll, then check, then close.
Step 4: after each single callback, go back to step 2.

explain.p: The nextTick added inside a promise callback (6) still runs before any timer. Node's internal loop is "drain ticks, run microtasks, check ticks again". Only when both are empty does it return to libuv.

The two timers are due at the same time, so they run in the same timers phase. Before Node 11, all timers in the phase ran first and the promise from timer 1 ran after both (output ...2, 4, 3). Since Node 11, Node drains microtasks between each timer callback, so the answer is ...2, 3, 4, the same as browsers.

explain.note: Say the version detail out loud. It shows you know the behavior changed and why: it was made consistent with browsers.

anim.title: Timers, promises and nested nextTick

steps.note: Synchronous: 1 prints.
Timer A is registered (it will log 2 and queue a promise).
Timer B is registered with the same delay, so it is due right after A.
A resolved promise: its callback (logs 5) enters the microtask queue.
A nextTick callback (logs 7) enters the nextTick queue.
Last synchronous line: 8 prints.
Stack is empty. nextTick queue goes first: 7.
Then the microtask queue: 5 prints.
The promise callback schedules a new nextTick. It goes into the nextTick queue, not the timers.
Node checks the nextTick queue again before leaving, so 6 prints before any timer.
Both small queues are empty. The loop enters the timers phase.
Timer A runs and prints 2.
Timer A queues a promise callback that logs 3.
Since Node 11, microtasks drain after each timer callback, so 3 prints before timer B.
Timer B runs and prints 4.
Everything is done and the process exits.

followups.q: What would Node 10 print?
followups.a: 1, 8, 7, 5, 6, 2, 4, 3. Old Node ran all expired timers in the phase first and drained microtasks only between phases.

followups.q: What if line 4 used process.nextTick instead of a promise?
followups.a: Same result: 3 still prints before 4, because the nextTick queue is also drained after each timer callback.

mistakes: Putting 6 after the timers because "it was scheduled later".
Answering 2, 4, 3 (the pre-Node-11 behavior) without mentioning the version.
Putting 5 before 7 in a CommonJS script.

questions.title: async/await under the hood
questions.question: How does async/await work under the hood? Where does the code after an await run? Then tell me what this prints.
questions.short: An async function runs synchronously until its first await. At the await, the function is suspended, the awaited value is wrapped in a promise, and the rest of the function is scheduled as a microtask that runs when that promise settles. The caller immediately gets a pending promise back. So code after await never runs in the same tick; it runs later in the microtask queue, after the current synchronous code and after pending nextTicks. Since V8 7.2 (Node 12), awaiting a native promise costs just one microtask tick.
questions.simple: await is a bookmark. The function puts a bookmark in, goes back to the caller, and continues from the bookmark later, when the awaited thing is ready.

explain.caption: A simplified mental model; V8 really uses a suspended generator-like state machine

list: Code before the first `await` runs synchronously, as part of the caller.
An `async` function always returns a promise, even if it returns a plain value or never awaits.
`await` on a non-promise value still yields: the rest runs in a microtask.
A `throw` inside an async function becomes a rejected promise, not a synchronous exception.
Returning a promise from an async function (`return somePromise`) adds extra microtask ticks compared to returning a value, because the outer promise has to adopt the inner one.

explain.p: await does not make code run in parallel and does not move work off the main thread. Two awaits in a row are sequential; use `Promise.all` for concurrency. And CPU-heavy code inside an async function still blocks the event loop.

explain.note: The microtask queue is shared. The continuation of an await is ordered with every other promise callback in FIFO order, which is what puzzles test.

anim.title: async/await ordering puzzle

steps.note: Synchronous log.
A timer is registered for the timers phase.
Calling a() runs its body synchronously up to the first await.
b() is called synchronously too. It logs and returns an already-resolved promise.
await suspends a(). Its continuation ("log a end") is queued as a microtask, and a() returns a pending promise to main.
A promise executor runs synchronously, right away.
The promise is resolved, so "then 1" is queued behind "resume a()". "then 2" waits for then 1's own promise.
A nextTick callback is queued.
Last synchronous line.
Stack is empty. nextTick queue drains first.
First microtask: a() resumes after the await and logs "a end".
then 1 runs. Its returned promise resolves, which queues then 2 at the back of the same microtask queue.
then 2 runs in the same drain, before any macrotask.
Only now does the loop reach the timers phase.

followups.q: Does an async function with no await still return asynchronously?
followups.a: Its body runs synchronously, but it returns a promise, and anything chained with .then or await on it runs in a later microtask.

followups.q: Is `return await p` different from `return p`?
followups.a: Inside try/catch, yes: only `return await` lets the catch handle a rejection. Outside try, the result is the same; `return await` also gives better async stack traces, and the extra tick no longer costs more in modern V8.

followups.q: How do you run awaits concurrently but limit the number?
followups.a: Use a small concurrency pool (for example p-limit, or a manual worker queue) instead of Promise.all on thousands of items.

mistakes: Thinking code before the first await runs asynchronously.
Believing await blocks the thread. It only suspends that one function.
Writing sequential awaits for independent calls and wondering why the endpoint is slow.

questions.title: Puzzle: inside an I/O callback
questions.question: Inside an fs.readFile callback I schedule a timeout, two setImmediates (the first one schedules a nextTick), a promise and a nextTick. What is the output?
questions.short: It prints: tick, promise, immediate 1, tick inside immediate, immediate 2, timeout. When the I/O callback returns, Node drains nextTick then microtasks. Poll is followed by check, so both immediates run before the timer. Microtasks and nextTicks drain after each immediate, so the tick from immediate 1 runs before immediate 2. The timer waits for the timers phase of the next loop turn.
questions.simple: Finish the I/O callback, clear the urgent lists, go next door to the setImmediate room and serve each guest (clearing urgent lists after each), then walk all the way around to the timers room.

list: The readFile callback runs in the poll phase. All five scheduling calls happen inside it.
When it returns: nextTick queue first (tick), then microtasks (promise).
Next phase is check. immediate 1 runs, and schedules a nextTick.
After each immediate callback, Node drains nextTick and microtasks, so "tick inside immediate" runs before immediate 2.
immediate 2 runs. The check phase is done; close callbacks; next turn starts with timers: timeout.

explain.p: This output is fully deterministic, unlike the same code at the top level of the main module, where the timer may or may not be ready when the loop starts.

explain.h: Why it is a good senior question

explain.p: It checks three things at once: phase order (poll, check, timers), the drain-after-each-callback rule, and nextTick priority over promises. If you can explain this one, the simpler puzzles are easy.

explain.note: If immediate 1 had called setImmediate again, that new callback would run on the next loop turn, after the timeout. setImmediate callbacks added during a check phase wait for the next check phase.

anim.title: Ordering inside a readFile callback

steps.note: The file read goes to the thread pool. The main script then ends.
The read completes. The loop picks up the callback in the poll phase.
Inside the poll phase now. A timer is registered.
immediate 1 is queued for the check phase.
immediate 2 is queued behind it.
A promise callback enters the microtask queue.
A nextTick callback enters the nextTick queue.
The I/O callback returns. nextTick queue drains first.
Then the microtask queue.
Poll is done. The next phase is check, so the immediates come before the timer.
immediate 1 runs.
It schedules a nextTick.
After each immediate callback, Node drains nextTicks and microtasks. So this runs before immediate 2.
immediate 2 runs.
Check is done. Close callbacks (none), then the loop wraps around to timers.
The timer finally runs.

followups.q: What changes if this code is at the top level instead of inside readFile?
followups.a: tick and promise still come first, but the timeout may run before or after the immediates, depending on whether 1 ms passed before the first timers phase.

followups.q: Where would a socket "close" handler fit?
followups.a: In the close callbacks phase, after check and before the next turn's timers, assuming the socket was destroyed earlier.

mistakes: Putting "tick inside immediate" after immediate 2, as if microtasks drain only between phases.
Putting timeout before the immediates because "setTimeout was called first".
Putting promise before tick.

questions.title: libuv thread pool
questions.question: Which operations use the libuv thread pool, which do not, and when would you change UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE?
questions.short: The thread pool runs work the OS cannot do asynchronously in a portable way: almost all fs operations, dns.lookup (getaddrinfo), async crypto like pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes, randomFill, generateKeyPair, and async zlib. Network sockets, pipes, TCP/UDP and dns.resolve* (c-ares) do not use it. The pool has 4 threads by default, shared by the whole process, so a few slow jobs can queue up everything else, for example slow DNS lookups delaying file reads. You can raise it with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE environment variable (max 1024) set before startup, when profiling shows pool saturation.
questions.simple: The thread pool is a kitchen with 4 cooks. If you send 5 slow dishes, the fifth waits, and so does every quick order behind it.

head: Uses the thread pool
Does not use it
rows: dns.lookup() (used by http.get with a hostname)
crypto.pbkdf2, scrypt, randomBytes(cb), randomFill, generateKeyPair, hkdf

explain.p: There is one pool per process, shared by all workers and all modules. If 4 slow `dns.lookup` calls are stuck (bad DNS server), every `fs.readFile` waits behind them. This is a classic hidden latency problem: your HTTP calls look slow but the real cause is queueing in the pool.

list: Set it as an environment variable before the process starts. Setting `process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` in code only works if it runs before anything touches the pool, which is fragile.
Bigger is not always better: more threads than CPU cores does not speed up CPU-bound work like pbkdf2; it helps mostly with I/O-bound waiting (slow disks, network file systems, DNS).
Each thread has its own stack memory, so very large values cost memory.
Cache DNS results or use `dns.resolve4` (no pool) for hosts you call often; enable HTTP keep-alive so you look up less.
Do CPU-heavy hashing in `worker_threads` or limit concurrency so it cannot fill the pool.
Stream big files instead of many parallel `readFile` calls.

explain.note: Fact to remember: both `fs.readFile` and `fs.createReadStream` use the thread pool and read in chunks (one pool request per chunk). The difference is memory: readFile holds the whole file in memory before calling you, while a stream lets each chunk be processed and freed.

anim.title: Five pbkdf2 jobs, four threads

steps.note: Job 1 is handed to libuv and starts on a pool thread.
Jobs 2 to 4 take the other three threads. The pool is now full.
Job 5 has no free thread, so it waits in libuv's work queue.
The JS thread is not blocked by any of this; it finishes the script.
One job finishes (the exact one varies). Its thread is freed and immediately picks up job 5.
In the poll phase the finished job's callback runs on the main thread.
Jobs 2 to 4 finish at about the same time. Job 5 started late, so it is still running.
Their callbacks run one after another.
Job 5 finishes last. It took about twice as long as the others because it queued for a thread.
The last callback runs, nothing is pending, and the process exits. With UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=5 all five would run at once (if there are enough cores).

followups.q: Why can slow DNS make file reads slow?
followups.a: dns.lookup and fs share the same 4-thread pool. If DNS calls hang, they hold threads and fs requests queue behind them.

followups.q: Does crypto.createHash use the thread pool?
followups.a: No. Hash, HMAC and cipher objects run synchronously on the main thread. Large hashing work blocks the loop, so stream data in chunks or use a worker.

followups.q: Do worker_threads have their own libuv thread pool?
followups.a: No. Each worker has its own event loop, but the libuv thread pool is shared by the whole process.

mistakes: Saying HTTP requests or database socket I/O use the thread pool.
Setting UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE inside a module after fs has already been used and expecting it to work.
Raising the pool to 128 to "speed up" CPU-bound hashing on a 4-core machine.

questions.title: Blocking the event loop
questions.question: What blocks the event loop, and how do you detect it in production?
questions.short: Anything that keeps the main thread busy for a long time blocks the loop: CPU-heavy loops, big JSON.parse or JSON.stringify, catastrophic regex backtracking, sync APIs like readFileSync or pbkdf2Sync, sorting huge arrays, or a nextTick/promise chain that never ends. While it runs, no timers, I/O callbacks or new requests are handled, so latency goes up for every user. I detect it with event loop delay (perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay, p99 and max), event loop utilization (performance.eventLoopUtilization), and then find the hot code with a CPU profile (--cpu-prof or the inspector).
questions.simple: If the only waiter stops to read a 500-page menu out loud, every other table waits, even the ones that only want water.

list: Sync APIs: `fs.readFileSync`, `crypto.pbkdf2Sync`, `zlib.gzipSync`, `child_process.execSync` in request paths.
`JSON.parse` / `JSON.stringify` of multi-megabyte payloads.
Regex with nested quantifiers on user input (ReDoS), for example `/(a+)+$/`.
Big loops, sorting or transforming large arrays in memory.
Unbounded `process.nextTick` or promise recursion (see starvation).
Long garbage collection pauses caused by large heaps or allocation spikes.

explain.caption: Export these as metrics (Prometheus, OpenTelemetry) instead of logging

list: Event loop delay (lag): how late a timer fires compared to when it should. A healthy API usually has p99 in low milliseconds; hundreds of ms means blocking.
Event loop utilization (ELU): fraction of time the loop is busy running code instead of idle in poll. Near 1.0 means the process is saturated; good signal for autoscaling.

explain.code:
node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./prof server.js   # writes .cpuprofile on exit
node --inspect server.js                          # attach Chrome DevTools, record a profile

explain.p: Open the `.cpuprofile` in Chrome DevTools (Performance tab) and look for wide frames on the main thread. Tools like Clinic.js (`clinic doctor`, `clinic flame`) automate this. For sync calls, `--trace-sync-io` prints a warning with a stack trace whenever a sync API is used after the first loop turn.

explain.note: Mention the user impact: a 200 ms block adds up to 200 ms to every request in flight at that moment, and health checks can time out, causing the orchestrator to restart a pod that is actually just busy.

anim.title: A 10 ms timer blocked for 200 ms

steps.note: The script starts and remembers the start time.
A timer is set to fire in 10 ms.
The busy loop starts. The JS thread can do nothing else while it spins.
The timer is now due, but it cannot run: the only JS thread is busy. In a server, new requests and I/O results would pile up too.
The blocking work ends after 200 ms.
The stack is empty, so the event loop can finally run. It goes to the timers phase.
The 10 ms timer runs about 190 ms late. That gap is exactly what "event loop delay" measures.

followups.q: How does monitorEventLoopDelay work?
followups.a: It uses a libuv timer sampling at the given resolution and records how late each sample fires into a histogram (values in nanoseconds). You read percentiles, mean, max.

followups.q: Is high ELU always bad?
followups.a: Not by itself; it means the process is busy. It is bad when combined with rising delay and latency. It is a good scaling signal because CPU usage can be misleading (GC and other threads count too).

followups.q: How do you protect against ReDoS?
followups.a: Avoid nested quantifiers on untrusted input, limit input length, test regexes with a safety checker, or use a linear-time engine (for example the re2 package) for user-supplied patterns.

mistakes: Looking only at CPU usage. A process can block on one core while total CPU looks moderate on a multi-core machine.
Wrapping CPU work in a Promise or async function and calling it non-blocking.
Using readFileSync in a request handler because "the file is small".

questions.title: Fixing CPU-heavy work
questions.question: You found a CPU-heavy function that blocks the loop for 300 ms per request. How do you fix it?
questions.short: First, check if the work is needed at all: cache it, precompute it, or do less (pagination, streaming). If it must run, I have three main options. Split it into small chunks and yield with setImmediate between chunks, so I/O can run in between; this keeps latency fair but does not add CPU. Move it to worker_threads with a pool (for example Piscina) so it runs in parallel on other cores. Or process data as a stream instead of loading it all at once. For very heavy jobs, push them to a queue and process them in a separate service.
questions.simple: Instead of one waiter doing a 30-minute job, either let him do one minute at a time between tables (chunking) or hire a helper in the back room (worker threads).

explain.h: Option 1: chunk and yield with setImmediate

explain.p: Use `setImmediate`, not `process.nextTick` or a resolved promise. nextTick and microtasks run before the loop continues, so they would not let any I/O in. setImmediate puts the next chunk after the poll phase of the next turn.

explain.caption: In production, reuse a pool of workers (e.g. Piscina) instead of one worker per request

list: Workers run JS in parallel on other cores. Starting one costs tens of milliseconds and memory, so use a pool.
Data is copied with the structured clone algorithm. Pass large binary data as transferable `ArrayBuffer`s, or share it with `SharedArrayBuffer`.
Size the pool near the number of cores (`os.availableParallelism()`).

explain.p: Parsing a 500 MB file with one `JSON.parse` blocks for seconds. Streaming it (line-delimited JSON with `readline`, or a streaming parser) and using `stream.pipeline` keeps each step small and keeps memory flat.

head: Technique
Good for
Trade-off
rows: Same total CPU, longer total time
Real CPU work: image, crypto, parsing

explain.note: Do not reach for cluster as the answer to a blocking function. More processes raise throughput, but each process still blocks its own requests during the 300 ms.

anim.title: Chunking lets other work in between

steps.note: The first chunk starts synchronously.
It handles only 2 items, then logs.
Instead of continuing, it schedules the next chunk with setImmediate and returns. The thread is free again.
Meanwhile, other work arrives (here a stand-in for another request).
Main is done. The loop runs timers and poll (I/O gets its chance), then the check phase.
Chunk 2 runs.
It queues chunk 3. A setImmediate added during the check phase waits for the next loop turn.
The other request is served in the middle of the long job. Without chunking it would wait for all of it.
A new loop turn: timers, then poll for any new I/O, then check again.
The last chunk runs and the job is complete.

followups.q: Why not chunk with Promise.resolve().then(next)?
followups.a: Microtasks are drained before the loop continues, so the chunks would run back to back with no I/O in between. It is still blocking, just split into pieces.

followups.q: When is a worker thread not worth it?
followups.a: For small tasks (a few milliseconds) the cost of messaging and copying data can be larger than the work itself. Batch work or keep it on the main thread.

followups.q: worker_threads vs child_process?
followups.a: Workers are lighter, share the process and can share memory. Child processes are fully isolated (a crash does not kill the parent) and can run any program.

mistakes: Chunking with process.nextTick or promises, which does not yield to I/O.
Creating a new Worker per request instead of using a pool.
Thinking cluster fixes the latency of a single blocking request.

questions.title: nextTick and microtask starvation
questions.question: Can process.nextTick or promises starve the event loop? Show me how and explain why setImmediate does not.
questions.short: Yes. Node drains the whole nextTick queue and the whole microtask queue before returning to the loop, including items added while draining. So a callback that keeps scheduling another nextTick, or a promise chain that keeps adding .then, never lets the loop reach timers, I/O or setImmediate; the process looks alive but serves nothing. setImmediate is safe for recursion because callbacks added during a check phase are deferred to the next loop turn, so I/O gets a chance in between.
questions.simple: If the "urgent" pile keeps getting a new urgent item every time you finish one, you never get to the normal mail.

explain.p: Node's internal drain logic is: run all nextTicks, run all microtasks, and repeat while anything is left. There is no limit per turn. Each new tick added while draining is processed in the same drain.

explain.h: Where it shows up in real life

list: A "retry until success" helper that retries with `await` but no delay, on an error that happens synchronously.
Recursive async processing of a large in-memory queue without any `await` on real I/O.
A stream or EventEmitter that re-emits synchronously in a loop.

explain.p: Symptoms: CPU is at 100% on one core, event loop delay grows without limit, timers never fire, and health checks time out. A CPU profile shows a tight cycle of nextTick or microtask frames.

explain.note: Rule of thumb: use nextTick and microtasks to defer a little work, never to loop. To loop over large work, use setImmediate (or a worker).

anim.title: nextTick recursion runs before any I/O

steps.note: An immediate is queued. Think of it as any I/O work waiting for the loop.
spin is queued in the nextTick queue.
Synchronous code finishes.
The stack is empty, so Node drains nextTicks. spin runs.
spin queues itself again. It goes into the same queue that is being drained right now.
Node keeps draining, so spin runs again. The loop still cannot move on.
And again it re-queues itself. Without the limit of 3, this would go on forever and the immediate would never run.
Third run: the limit is hit and it stops scheduling.
Only now, with the nextTick queue empty, can the loop continue to its phases.
The check phase finally runs the immediate.

followups.q: Is there a maximum nextTick depth in Node?
followups.a: Not anymore. Old Node versions had process.maxTickDepth; it was removed. Today the queue is drained without a limit.

followups.q: Would await in a loop starve the loop?
followups.a: Only if every awaited value is already resolved (no real I/O). Then each iteration is just a microtask and the loop never yields. Awaiting real I/O does yield.

mistakes: Assuming promises "yield to the event loop" like setTimeout does.
Using recursive nextTick for long-running iteration.
Expecting timers to fire while a microtask loop is running.

questions.title: Process lifecycle, ref and unref
questions.question: What happens from `node app.js` until the process exits? Why does a process sometimes stay alive, and what do ref() and unref() do?
questions.short: Node starts V8 and libuv, bootstraps its internals, loads app.js (resolving and running required modules, which are cached), and runs the main module synchronously. Then it drains nextTick and microtasks and enters the event loop. The loop keeps running while there are active, referenced handles (servers, sockets, timers, child processes) or pending requests (fs, dns). When none remain, Node emits beforeExit, and if nothing new is scheduled it emits exit and the process ends. unref() tells the loop not to count a handle, so it no longer keeps the process alive; ref() undoes that.
questions.simple: The loop is a shop that stays open while at least one customer is inside. An unref'd timer is like a cleaner: he can be there, but the shop does not stay open just for him.

list: Process start: initialize V8, the libuv loop, the thread pool (lazily), signal handlers, options and env.
Bootstrap: run Node's internal JS to set up `process`, globals, and the module loaders.
Load the main module: CommonJS wraps the file in a function `(exports, require, module, __filename, __dirname)` and runs it; ESM is parsed, linked, then evaluated.
Main module finishes: nextTick and microtask queues are drained.
Event loop: `uv_run` runs phases while the loop is alive.
Loop empty: `process` emits `beforeExit`. If a listener schedules new work, the loop continues.
Exit: `process` emits `exit` (only sync code works there), then the process ends with `process.exitCode` (default 0).

explain.p: Active referenced handles: a listening server, an open socket, a pending timer or interval, a child process, a `process.stdin` in flowing mode, a worker. Plus in-flight requests like an fs read. A frequent bug: an open DB pool or a `setInterval` keeps a CLI script or a test runner from exiting.

explain.h: process.exit() vs letting the loop drain

explain.p: `process.exit()` ends the process right away: stdout writes that are still pending (they are sometimes asynchronous), in-flight requests, and `beforeExit` are skipped. For servers, prefer a graceful shutdown: on SIGTERM, call `server.close()`, close DB pools, set `process.exitCode`, and let the loop empty naturally, with a fallback timer (unref'd) that forces exit if shutdown hangs.

explain.note: beforeExit is not emitted when you call process.exit() or when there is an uncaught exception. Do not put critical cleanup only there.

anim.title: What keeps the loop alive

steps.note: Node boots V8 and libuv, runs its internal bootstrap, wraps app.js in the CommonJS module function and calls it.
The main module runs synchronously.
An interval is created. By default every timer is ref'd: it keeps the process alive.
unref() keeps the timer running but tells the loop not to count it when deciding whether to stay alive.
A normal 20 ms timeout is ref'd.
Listeners for beforeExit and exit are registered. Listeners themselves do not keep the loop alive.
The main module finishes.
The loop starts. It is alive because one ref'd handle (the timeout) exists. It sleeps in poll until the timer is due.
After 20 ms the timeout fires. A one-shot timer is done after it runs, so it is no longer an active handle.
Only an unref'd handle is left, so the loop is no longer alive. The interval never gets to fire.
Node emits beforeExit. The listener schedules nothing new, so Node goes on to exit.
The exit event fires with the exit code. Only synchronous code can run here; the loop is gone.

followups.q: My test runner hangs after tests finish. How do you debug it?
followups.a: Something still holds a ref'd handle: an open DB pool, server, or interval. Use process.getActiveResourcesInfo() or a tool like why-is-node-running, then close it in teardown (or unref background timers).

followups.q: What happens if you schedule a timer inside a beforeExit listener?
followups.a: The loop becomes alive again and keeps running. When it empties again, beforeExit fires again, so be careful not to create an infinite cycle.

followups.q: Can you run async work in the exit handler?
followups.a: No. By the time exit fires, the event loop has stopped. Only synchronous work runs; anything async is dropped.

mistakes: Calling process.exit() right after writing logs. Writes to stdout are sometimes asynchronous (it depends on the platform and whether stdout is a file, terminal or pipe), so the last lines can be lost.
Doing async cleanup in an exit listener.
Thinking event listeners (process.on, emitter.on) keep the process alive. Handles and requests do, listeners do not.
